note: Use these senses exactly. Do not invent alternatives.

terms.sense: A new text written from a source text for a form, audience and purpose the task sets, re-using the source’s content.
terms.boundary: Not a summary of the source, and not a copy of its wording.

terms.sense: An analysis of the similarities and differences between two texts, each explained by the texts’ purposes, audiences and contexts.
terms.boundary: In Paper 1 Question 1(b) the two texts are the source and your own directed response.

terms.sense: A structured account of how a text’s form, structure and language make meaning for its audience.
The Paper 2 Question 1(a) task: a text of no more than 400 words written to a brief.
An analysis of your own text’s choices of form, structure and language and how they fulfil the brief.
terms.boundary: It analyses choices; it does not retell what your text says.

terms.sense: The Paper 2 Section B task: one continuous piece of 600–900 words in one of three categories.
The specification a piece of writing must meet: its form, audience, purpose, role and any focus the prompt adds.
The kind of text a piece is, such as an article, a speech, an email or a review, with the conventions its readers expect.
terms.boundary: In grammar, “form” can also mean the shape of a word; in this subject it means the kind of text unless a block says otherwise.

terms.sense: The features readers expect of a form, such as a headline in an article or a salutation in a letter.
A family of texts grouped by shared purpose and conventions.
terms.boundary: Wider than form: travel writing is a genre that can take the form of a blog, an article or a book.

terms.sense: The readers or listeners a text is designed for, stated or implied.
The reader a text’s choices assume, who may differ from the people who actually read it.
What a text sets out to do, such as inform, persuade, entertain, advise or argue; many texts have more than one.
The situation a text is produced and read in: when, where, by whom, for whom and through what medium.
terms.boundary: In analysis it can also mean the words around a quotation; say which sense you mean.

terms.sense: The features that make a text recognisably the kind of text it is.
The overall manner of a text, produced by its choices of form, structure and language together.
terms.boundary: Distinct from tone, which is the attitude a text conveys.

terms.sense: Writing that presents itself as true: articles, memoirs, reviews, speeches, letters, travel writing.
terms.boundary: Non-fiction can use narrative techniques without becoming fiction.

terms.sense: The grammatical category of a word by the job it does: noun, verb, adjective, adverb, pronoun, determiner, preposition, conjunction.
terms.boundary: Also called parts of speech.

terms.sense: A word that names a person, place, thing or idea.
A noun for something that can be perceived by the senses.
A noun for an idea, quality or state.
A word for an action, a process or a state.
A word that describes or modifies a noun.
A word that modifies a verb, an adjective, another adverb or a whole clause.
A word that stands in for a noun phrase, such as she, we, they or it.
terms.boundary: Inclusive pronouns (we, us) place writer and reader on the same side.

terms.sense: A word that introduces a noun and specifies it, such as the, a, this or every.
A word or phrase that adds detail to another; a premodifier comes before a noun, a postmodifier after it.
The vocabulary of a text, and the choices a writer makes from it.
A group of words in a text from one area of meaning, such as war or illness.
terms.boundary: Also called a lexical field.

terms.sense: The literal, dictionary meaning of a word.
The associations a word carries beyond its literal meaning.
terms.boundary: Analysis names the specific association, not only whether it is favourable.

terms.sense: Language that means more than, or other than, its literal sense.
A figure that describes one thing as if it were another, without “like” or “as”.
A comparison of one thing with another using “like” or “as”.
Giving human qualities or actions to something that is not human.
terms.boundary: Not every vivid image is personification: it needs a human quality.

terms.sense: Weather or surroundings described so that they mirror a character’s feelings or a mood.
Language that creates a picture or sensation in the reader’s mind, literal or figurative.
The sound of language; in a written text, patterns such as alliteration, assonance, sibilance and onomatopoeia.
Repetition of the same consonant sound at the start of nearby words.
Repetition of hissing s and sh sounds.
A word whose sound imitates what it names.
How words are built from smaller parts: roots, prefixes, suffixes, compounds and coinages.
A newly made word, often a compound, used for effect.
Whether a clause is active (the doer is the subject) or passive (the thing acted on is the subject).
terms.boundary: Not the same as a writer’s voice: see “voice (writer’s)”.

terms.sense: The sense of a particular person speaking, carried by what they notice and how they say it.
terms.boundary: Not grammatical voice.

terms.sense: A construction in which the thing acted on becomes the subject, and the doer is moved to a “by” phrase or left out.
How a verb presents an action in time: progressive (ongoing, “was running”) or perfect (completed, “has run”).
The form of a verb that places an action in past or present time.
terms.boundary: The present tense can narrate past events for immediacy.

terms.sense: The expression of certainty, possibility, obligation or permission, through modal verbs (may, must, could) and adverbs (perhaps, certainly).
terms.boundary: High modality sounds sure; low modality sounds tentative.

terms.sense: The arrangement of words, phrases and clauses in a sentence.
A sentence with one main clause.
Two or more main clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction such as and, but or so.
A sentence with a main clause and at least one subordinate clause.
A deliberate sentence without a main verb, used for effect.
terms.boundary: Distinct from an accidental fragment.

terms.sense: Moving a word or phrase to the start of a sentence to give it prominence.
A group of three parallel words, phrases or clauses.
terms.boundary: Also called a list of three or a triad.

terms.sense: How a whole text is organised: its opening, sequence, shifts of focus, paragraphing and ending.
terms.boundary: Sentence structure is a feature of language; “structure” alone means the whole text.

terms.sense: The ties that link sentences and paragraphs, such as discourse markers, reference and repetition.
A word or phrase that signals how a text moves on, such as however, meanwhile or in short.
A word that points back to something already mentioned, such as “this” or “she”.
A word that points forward to something not yet named.
A structure in which the ending returns to the opening.
The position from which a story or account is told: first person, second person, or third person limited or omniscient.
Telling from inside, as “I”, limited to what that narrator knows.
terms.boundary: Not the same as stream of consciousness.

terms.sense: Narration that follows a mind’s flow of thoughts and associations without ordinary ordering.
terms.boundary: Rare in the papers; do not use it for ordinary first-person writing.

terms.sense: Third-person narration that can enter any character’s mind and know anything.
A technique of persuasive language, such as a rhetorical question, anaphora, antithesis, tricolon or direct address.
A question asked for effect, whose answer is assumed rather than sought.
terms.boundary: A question the text goes on to answer, or that the reader must answer, is not rhetorical.

terms.sense: Speaking to the reader or listener as “you”.
Repetition of a word or phrase at the start of successive clauses or sentences.
terms.boundary: In grammar, “anaphoric reference” is a different idea.

terms.sense: Opposed ideas placed side by side in parallel form.
Deliberate exaggeration.
The attitude a text conveys towards its subject or its reader, such as urgent, wry or reassuring.
terms.boundary: Tone is a result of choices; name the choices that create it.

terms.sense: The variety of language suited to a situation, marked chiefly by its formality and its vocabulary.
terms.boundary: Distinct from tone: a text can be formal in register and warm in tone.

terms.sense: How far a text’s language follows the conventions of formal, public usage rather than casual, private usage.
terms.boundary: Not the same as how common or rare a word is.

terms.sense: The study of meaning that comes from context and implication, not from the words alone.
What a speaker or writer implies without stating it.
The exact words from a text that show the feature a point is about.
A short quotation worked into the grammar of your own sentence.
What a choice leads the reader to think, feel or do.
terms.boundary: Distinct from the meaning of the words.

terms.sense: Naming features without analysing what they do.
The sentence, usually first, that states what a paragraph is about.
The detail, example or explanation that carries a point or a moment further.
A model of plot in five stages: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution.
The opening stage of a story, which sets out the situation, the characters and the setting.
The point of greatest tension in a story, where the conflict comes to a head.
How a story’s conflict is settled, or deliberately left open, after the climax.
Tension created by making the reader wait to learn what will happen.
Writing that builds a picture of a place, moment or experience from detail, not from a sequence of events.
Writing that tells a story: characters, a sequence of events and a change.
Writing that explores an issue from more than one side before reaching a view.
Writing that argues for one position, answering the other side on the way.
An argument built from a view (thesis), its opposite (antithesis) and a reasoned resolution (synthesis).
A point against your position.
An answer to a counterargument that shows why it does not outweigh your case.
Granting that part of an opposing point is true.
An informed judgement of a work, product, event or place, for readers deciding whether to try it.
The standards a review judges by, such as value, quality or suitability.
The link between a judgement and the specific evidence that supports it.
Vocabulary that expresses a judgement, from mild to strong.
Two complete sentences joined by a comma alone.
